system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 12 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-08-17 21:25:00 to 2184-08-29 12:35:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of gastroparesis and J-tube placement was readmitted one day after discharge due to a recurrent flare of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. She was unable to tolerate oral intake or tube feeds initially. In the ED, she received IV fluids, lorazepam, and morphine, with improvement in symptoms. Admission labs showed mild hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis, both of which resolved with hydration. A contrast study confirmed proper J-tube placement without complications. Over the hospital stay, she gradually tolerated advancing tube feeds, discontinued IV medications, and resumed oral medications via the tube. Given her recent frequent hospitalizations, she was discharged with crushed lorazepam and morphine tablets to administer through her J-tube during future flares, along with follow-up appointments. She was ambulatory and stable at discharge.

regarding the need for exploratory laparotomy, and consent was 
obtained. In addition, the patient had a gastric pacemaker

right side of the abdomen, and a discussion was had about 
possible excision of the gastric pacemaker and wires. NG tube, 
Foley, and IV fluid resuscitation was initiated, and IV 
antibiotics were given.

The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, right 
hemicolectomy, stapled ileotransverse anastomosis, repair of 
stomach, and excision of gastric pacemaker, with 2 wires and 2 
plastic buttons with 2 clips each per button, which went well 
without complication (reader referred to the Operative Note for

patient arrived on the floor NPO with NGT, on IV fluids, and PCA 
for pain control.  The patient was hemodynamically stable.

patient voided without problem. On POD#5 the patient went to ___ 
for exchange ___ tube for a MIC GJ tube. The patient had 
return of bowel function and tubefeeds were restarted on POD#6.

however the patient had ongoing nausea and was unable to 
tolerate GT clampings or regular diet. On POD#9 GT clamping 
trials were again attempted with better results. On POD#10 the 
patient went for a gastric emptying study which was normal and 
for an upper GI swallow study to evaluate her Nissen 
fundiplication which showed no stricture but did show esophageal 
dysmotility.

diet with good tolerability. ___ evaluated the patient and 
cleared her for home. During this hospitalization, the patient 
ambulated early and frequently, was adherent with respiratory 
toilet and incentive spirometry, and actively participated in 
the plan of care. The patient received subcutaneous heparin and 
venodyne boots were used during this stay.

with stable vital signs. The patient was tolerating a regular 
diet, tolerating tubefeeds at goal, ambulating, voiding without

Ms ___,

You were admitted to ___ with abdominal pain and were found to 
have cecal volvulus with evidence of ischemia, which was caused 
by your gastric pacer leads tangling in your bowels.  You were 
taken to the operating room and underwent an exploratory 
laparotomy, right hemi-colectomy, repair of the stomach, and 
removal of the gastric pacer wires. You tolerated the procedure 
well. Post-operatively, you continued to have nausea and 
inability to tolerate your tube feeds, which slowly resolved.  
You went for a gastric emptying study, which was normal and did 
not show any delayed gastric emptying. You also went for an 
upper GI study to evaluate your ___ fundoplication site. This 
study showed the ___ Fundoplication site was unremarkable 
without evidence of narrowing, however there was there was a 
question of esophageal dysmotility. You should follow-up with 
your Gastroenterologist to have an outpatient work-up for this. 
You have tolerated a regular diet and your tubefeeds are at 
goal. Your nausea has improved and you are ready to return home 
to continue your recovery. Please note the following discharge 
instructions:

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:
*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.
*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.
*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.
*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.
*You see blood or dark/black material when you vomit or have a 
bowel movement.
*You experience burning when you urinate, have blood in your 
urine, or experience a discharge.
*Your pain in not improving within ___ hours or is not gone 
within 24 hours. Call or return immediately if your pain is 
getting worse or changes location or moving to your chest or 
back.
*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.
*Any change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that concern 
you.

Please resume all regular home medications, unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.

Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids. Avoid lifting 
weights greater than ___ lbs until you follow-up with your 
surgeon.

Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking pain 
medications.

Incision Care:
*Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner if you have 
increased pain, swelling, redness, or drainage from the incision 
site.
*Avoid swimming and baths until your follow-up appointment.
*You may shower, and wash surgical incisions with a mild soap 
and warm water. Gently pat the area dry.
*If you have staples, they will be removed at your follow-up 
appointment.
*If you have steri-strips, they will fall off on their own.

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:
*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.
*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.
*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.
*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.
*You see blood or dark/black material when you vomit or have a 
bowel movement.
*You experience burning when you urinate, have blood in your 
urine, or experience a discharge.
*Your pain in not improving within ___ hours or is not gone 
within 24 hours. Call or return immediately if your pain is 
getting worse or changes location or moving to your chest or 
back.
*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.
*Any change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that concern 
you.

Please resume all regular home medications, unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.

Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids. Avoid lifting 
weights greater than ___ lbs until you follow-up with your 
surgeon.

Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking pain 
medications.

Incision Care:
*Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner if you have 
increased pain, swelling, redness, or drainage from the incision 
site.
*Avoid swimming and baths until your follow-up appointment.
*You may shower, and wash surgical incisions with a mild soap 
and warm water. Gently pat the area dry.
*If you have staples, they will be removed at your follow-up 
appointment.
*If you have steri-strips, they will fall off on their own. 
Please remove any remaining strips ___ days after surgery.

 
Followup Instructions:
___

EXAMINATION:  CT ABD AND PELVIS WITH CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with gastroparesis p/w intractable N/V x2 days,
no BM or flatus x2 days.  Presence of obstructionPlease give with PO and IV
contrast

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were obtained from the lung bases to the pubic
symphysis after the administration of 130 cc of intravenous contrast.  Axial
images were interpreted in conjunction with coronal and sagittal reformats. 
Oral contrast was administered.

DLP:  442.50 mGy-cm

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen/pelvis ___.

FINDINGS: 

CHEST:  Limited assessment of lung bases demonstrates right lower lobe
atelectasis.  No pleural effusion. The visualized heart is normal in size
without pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

The liver is homogeneous in enhancement. No focal lesion identified.No
intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilatation. Patient is status post
cholecystectomy with clips in the gallbladder fossa. The portal vein, SMV, and
splenic vein are patent.

The spleen is normal. The pancreas enhances homogenously and is without focal
lesions, peripancreatic fat stranding, or focal fluid collection. The right
adrenal gland is normal. Again seen is a small left adrenal nodule measuring
1.1 x 1.3 cm (02:21), unchanged from previous examination.

The kidneys display symmetric nephrograms and excretion of contrast.  A 2.5 x
2.6 cm (2: 29) cyst is seen within the interpolar region of the right kidney,
slightly larger from previous examination (previously 1.8 x 1.9 cm). No
hydronephrosis or hydroureter identified.  No renal or proximal ureter
calculi.  Mild focal urothelial thickening on the right proximal ureter
(2:34).  Also, over ___ years there is new soft tissue, probably nodal,
along the course of the proximal right renal artery, measuring up to about 31
x 17 mm including the artery (which is not at all narrowed).  A few borderline
nearby discrete nodules, hyperenhancing, are also present.

Patient is status post fundoplication. Again seen is a percutaneous
gastrojejunostomy tube entering in the left upper quadrant, extending to the
proximal jejunum in the left upper quadrant. The stomach is otherwise grossly
unremarkable in appearance. The small bowel is normal in caliber without wall
thickening.  The cecum is within the left upper quadrant with ileocecal valve
along its medial aspect. Swirling of the mesentery is noted within the right
lower quadrant consistent with a cecal volvulus.  Possible lead point includes
loop of patient's gastric pacemaker given that it makes a loop apparently
around the mesentery on which the cecum is suspected.  Curvilinear swirling
appearance to the metallic lead follows the course of the mesentery (601b:
24). The remaining distal colon is decompressed. Mesenteric fat stranding and
cecal bowel wall edema is noted. (601 b: 26). No pneumatosis. No extraluminal
air. No pneumoperitoneum. No portal venous gas. Colonic diverticulosis is
present without evidence of acute diverticulitis. The appendix is not
visualized.  The gastric pacer device is seated in anterior soft tissues.

The abdominal aorta is normal in caliber without aneurysmal dilatation. 
Stable appearance of chronic focal dissection within the midportion of the
superior mesenteric artery with good distal vessel opacification, and is
slightly more lateral on today's examination from cecal volvulus.  The celiac
axis, SMA, and ___ are otherwise patent . Moderate amount of atherosclerotic
calcification noted. The iliac arteries are normal in course and caliber.

No retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymph node enlargement by CT size criteria.
Small amount of mesenteric fluid identified.  No abdominal wall hernia.

PELVIS: The bladder is well distended and normal. No pelvic side-wall or
inguinal lymph node enlargement by CT size criteria.  Trace free pelvic fluid
seen.  The uterus is small or absent.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES: Multilevel, multifactorial degenerative changes are seen
within the visualized thoracolumbar spine. No focal lytic or sclerotic lesion
concerning for malignancy.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Cecal volvulus with evidence of ischemia including fat stranding, wall
edema, and mesenteric free fluid. No pneumatosis. The lead point may represent
the metallic lead from implanted device.

2.  Stable left adrenal nodule.

3.  Stable chronic focal SMA dissection with good distal SMA opacification. 
This is a chronic finding with no luminal compromise.

4.  New focal lymphadenopathy along the upper right retroperitoneum, including
soft tissue along the right renal artery.  This is of uncertain etiology and
significance.  Correlation with any history of known malignancy is
recommended.  PET-CT or alternatively short-term follow-up chest CT including
the area is suggested to reassess and also to assess for any lymph nodes
elsewhere.

5.  Mild urothelial thickening on the right proximal ureter.  Correlate with
urinalysis.

NOTIFICATION:   The findings were discussed by Dr. ___ with Dr.

Dr. ___ discussed the issue of new retroperitoneal abnormality
requiring non-urgent work-up after acute illness with Dr. ___ on ___, by telephone.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with newly placed R IJ CVL  // eval CVL 
Contact name: ___, ___: ___

FINDINGS: 

Recently placed right internal jugular catheter terminates in the mid superior
vena cava, with no pneumothorax.  Appearance of the chest is otherwise
unchanged since ___ except for new foci of linear atelectasis in both

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with ___ G-J tube  // exchange ___ for

COMPARISON:  GJ tube exchange from ___.

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATOR: Dr. ___ radiology attending)
performed the procedure.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of

MEDICATIONS: None

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and

Patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team. I know you’ve been having severe abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me more about what brought you in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had terrible cramping for two days—no bowel movements, no gas. I couldn’t keep anything down, not even through my tube. It felt worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of gastroparesis and a feeding tube. We did a CT scan, and it showed something serious—your cecum, part of your colon, has twisted. That’s called a cecal volvulus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Twisted? Is that why I couldn’t pass anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The twist is blocking your bowel. Worse, the blood supply is compromised—there’s early signs of ischemia. This needs surgery, and soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? Again? I’ve had so many… What kind of surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do an exploratory laparotomy. We’ll remove the twisted part of your colon—the right side—and reconnect your intestine. There’s also something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT suggests the wires from your old gastric pacemaker may have caused the twist. They’re looping into your bowel. We’ll remove the device and wires during the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I forgot I even had that pacemaker. Is it dangerous to remove?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s safe, and necessary. Leaving it could cause more problems. We’ve discussed this with your family, and we have your consent. We’ll prepare you for the OR now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through surgery. You had a right hemicolectomy and the pacemaker with its wires was removed. The anastomosis looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I feel? I’m so groggy… Was everything okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgery went well—no complications. You’re on a PCA pump for pain. You have an NG tube for now, and we’re giving fluids and antibiotics through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to wait for your bowel to wake up. We’ll start tube feeds once we hear bowel sounds and you pass gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your NG tube is out. You’re passing gas, and your belly is less distended. We’ll keep you NPO for now, but we’re close to starting feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My throat was so sore from the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count was high but is coming down. That means the infection risk is improving. We’re still holding off on feeds—just a little longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start your tube feeds today—slowly, at half goal. We’ll monitor for nausea or bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m still feeling a bit nauseous. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially after surgery and with your history. We’ll give you anti-nausea meds and go slow. If you tolerate this, we’ll increase tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well with the feeds. We’re increasing to full rate. Your labs are stable, and you’re walking more each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today, we’re exchanging your GJ tube to one with separate G and J ports. It’ll give us more flexibility with feeding and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a big procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s done endoscopically with light sedation. You’ll be back soon, and we’ll restart feeds through the new tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube exchange went smoothly. You’re back on full feeds. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit sore at the site, but okay. Still nauseous when I try to eat by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expected that. We’re going to try clamping your tube for short periods to see if you can tolerate oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve always had trouble keeping food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we need to assess if it’s mechanical or motility-related. We’ll schedule a gastric emptying study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gastric emptying study came back normal. Liquids are leaving your stomach at a normal rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why do I feel so full and nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an upper GI study too. It shows your Nissen fundoplication is intact, no narrowing. But there’s moderate esophageal dysmotility—your esophagus isn’t moving food down well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my stomach, it’s my esophagus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That explains the nausea when you try to eat. We’ll adjust your diet and add a new anti-nausea med. You’ll follow up with GI after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating clamping trials better. We’re advancing your diet to regular food in small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a few bites yesterday and didn’t vomit. That’s progress!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your incision is healing well—no redness or drainage. Pain is controlled with oral meds now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’re walking independently, tolerating a regular diet, and your feeds are at goal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your labs are stable, vitals are good. Home health will help with your GJ tube and feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue levothyroxine, citalopram, omeprazole. We’re adding dronabinol and trimethobenzamide for nausea, as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your surgeon in two weeks. GI will evaluate your esophageal dysmotility. Call us if you have fever, vomiting, or incision problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about lifting or driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lifting over five pounds for four weeks. Don’t drive while on pain meds. Showering is okay—just keep the incision dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the steri-strips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll fall off on their own. Remove any left after ten days. Staples will be removed at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about managing the tube at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Home health will train you and your caregiver. They’ll visit several times a week at first. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel more confident now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep resting, stay hydrated, and keep walking. You’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, you’re tolerating everything well. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t wait to be home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be here if you need us. Take care, and see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I get the flu shot this year?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. It’s especially important with your medical history. Your primary care can give it in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’ll schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Rest well, and don’t hesitate to call with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned that the hard way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re doing great. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and meds shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Call us if anything’s unclear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for being so thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s our job. You’ve been a great patient—cooperative and strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been a lot, but I’m glad it’s over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you came through it well. Recovery will take time, but you’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll miss you, but we’re glad you’re going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll miss you all too. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been our privilege. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of gastroparesis, gastrostomy, and a gastric pacemaker was admitted for severe abdominal pain and vomiting. Imaging revealed cecal volvulus with ischemia, likely caused by entanglement of the bowel with the pacemaker wires. She underwent an exploratory laparotomy, right hemicolectomy, ileotransverse anastomosis, stomach repair, and removal of the gastric pacemaker and wires. Postoperatively, she had ongoing nausea and difficulty tolerating oral intake, but gradually improved with tube feeds and diet advancement. A gastric emptying study was normal, but an upper GI series showed moderate esophageal dysmotility. She tolerated a regular diet and full tube feeds by discharge, with stable vital signs and healing incisions. She was discharged home with home health services for GJ tube care and follow-up with gastroenterology for esophageal evaluation.
